title: Docker Images
subtitle: Layers, tags, digests and the local image store
description: Understand what an image really contains, how layers are shared, and how to inspect and manage the local store without wasting disk.
outcomes: Read image metadata, history and digests
Understand layer sharing and cache implications
Tag, pull, save and prune images safely

modules.title: The image model
modules.summary: What is inside an image and how it is stored.

lessons.title: Image anatomy and layers
lessons.summary: An image is a manifest, a config and a stack of content-addressed layers.

sections.title: Not a tarball
sections.body:
An image is a manifest that references a config JSON and a list of layer blobs. Each layer is a diff of the filesystem. The config holds environment, entrypoint, command, labels, exposed ports, and the history of build instructions.

At runtime, the layers are composed into a read-only root filesystem and a writable layer is added. Writes use copy-on-write: modifying a file copies it into the writable layer, leaving the image layer untouched.

sections.caption: Shared read-only layers beneath a per-container writable layer.

sections.code:
docker image inspect nginx:alpine --format '{{json .RootFS.Layers}}'
docker image history --no-trunc nginx:alpine
docker image inspect nginx:alpine --format '{{.Config.Env}}'

sections.title: Layer IDs are content hashes
sections.body: Identical instructions on identical inputs produce identical layers. This is why layer order and reproducibility matter.

exercises.title: Count layers
exercises.prompt: Print the number of layers in nginx:alpine.
exercises.command: docker image inspect nginx:alpine --format '{{json .RootFS.Layers}}' | jq length
exercises.expected: Pipe RootFS.Layers to jq length or count the JSON entries.

exercises.title: Read history
exercises.prompt: Find the instruction that set the nginx entrypoint.
exercises.expected: docker image history --no-trunc shows the ENTRYPOINT instruction.

questions.question: What does an image manifest reference?
questions.explain: The manifest points at the config and content-addressed layers.

questions.question: How are layers shared between images?
questions.explain: The same layer blob is reused by digest.

questions.question: What is the writable layer?
options: A per-container layer created at runtime
questions.explain: Each container gets its own writable layer.

lessons.title: Pull, inspect and tag
lessons.summary: Daily image operations with attention to tags, digests and registry defaults.

sections.title: Pull behaviour
sections.body: `docker pull` fetches the manifest and missing layers. `--platform` selects an architecture when the image is multi-platform. A pull can be refused because of authentication, rate limits, or a missing tag. The error names the registry and repository; read it literally.

sections.code:
docker pull --platform linux/amd64 nginx:1.27-alpine
docker image inspect nginx:1.27-alpine --format '{{.Architecture}} {{.Os}}'
docker tag nginx:1.27-alpine registry.example.com/web/nginx:1.27-alpine
docker image ls --filter reference='registry.example.com/*'
sections.output:
amd64 linux
REPOSITORY                          TAG            IMAGE ID       SIZE
registry.example.com/web/nginx       1.27-alpine    ...            48.2MB

sections.title: Tag is local until you push
sections.body: `docker tag` only creates another name for the same image ID locally. `docker push` publishes it to the registry named in the tag.

exercises.title: Read labels
exercises.prompt: Inspect the labels of an official image.

questions.question: Does docker tag upload the image?
options: No, it only adds a local name

questions.question: Which flag selects an architecture on a multi-platform image?
A pull fails with "manifest unknown". What is wrong?
options: The tag or repository does not exist
questions.explain: The registry has no manifest for that reference.

lessons.title: Cleanup, save and prune
lessons.summary: Reclaim disk with confidence and move images between isolated environments.
objectives: Prune without deleting what you need

sections.title: Know what is reclaimable
sections.body: `docker system df` reports Size and Reclaimable per object type. Dangling images (`<none>:<none>`) are intermediate or untagged layers. Unused images are not referenced by any container. Build cache is often the largest consumer.

sections.code:
docker system df
docker image ls --filter dangling=true
docker image prune          # dangling only
docker image prune -a       # all unused images
docker builder prune
docker system prune --volumes

docker save -o app.tar acme/app:1.0
docker load -i app.tar
sections.output:
TYPE            TOTAL     ACTIVE    SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
Images          107       10        101.4GB   61.28GB (60%)
Build Cache     1089      0         66.72GB   41.33GB (62%)

sections.title: Prune is not undoable
sections.body: Containers created later cannot use a deleted image without re-pulling. In air-gapped environments, export important images first.

exercises.title: Reclaim safely
exercises.prompt: Show reclaimable space, then remove only dangling images.
exercises.command: docker system df && docker image prune -f
exercises.expected: docker system df followed by docker image prune.

exercises.title: Air-gap transfer
exercises.prompt: Save alpine:3.20 to a file and load it after removing it locally.
exercises.expected: docker save -o alpine.tar alpine:3.20; docker load -i alpine.tar

questions.question: What is a dangling image?
questions.explain: Dangling images are untagged (<none>:<none>) and safe to prune.

questions.question: Which command transfers an image without a registry?
questions.explain: Save writes a tar archive; load imports it.
